en: The Intertwining of the *Huayan* Dharma-Characteristics (with Preface), by Daotong, who lectured on the sutras at Nanren Garden in the Eastern Capital.

When the Great Awakened One manifested his parinirvāṇa, the sun of the Dharma sank its radiance. Teachings follow the differences in capacities; they cannot be restricted to a single fixed interpretation. Nature and characteristics mutually support one another.

His vision was perfect and subtle; (Dao Tong) had long been attached to the True Vehicle. Dwelling in seclusion at the lecture hall, he expounded and listened to the teachings, bringing great benefit.

As the sutras transmitted the wondrous emptiness, he withdrew in shame, feeling he could neither emulate the sages of old nor assist the students of later generations. Having repeatedly endured hardships and calamities, he felt all the more that his faculties were failing.
He built a dwelling south of the city to merely prolong his years, yet two or three scholars did not abandon him, and day by day they made his lecture seat their own.

Regarding this matter, while perusing an old chest, I obtained the treatise on the meaning of the Dharma entitled *Pánjié* (The Knots). Within it, the aspects of defilement and purity are fused; the conditions for reliance and the principles of increase and reduction are detailed;

the essence of pride and its varieties are analyzed; and the provisional self and provisional dharmas are examined. It contains subtle words concerning the three objects and five fruits, and wondrous explanations regarding the four conditions and ten causes.
It elucidates the expressive and non-expressive [forms] of both specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and is based upon principle...
Based on the differences between objects, there arises the distinction between mistaking a tree stump for a person and mistaking a person for a tree stump.

This can truly be called the principle of "twisted roots and knotted joints," and the literary style of "jingling gold and vibrating jade. One might know it without formal study; yet, having merely heard its words, one has not yet seen the man behind them.
It is not that I wish to establish a school of my own, but rather to use this to settle the inquiries of students. May those of like mind not laugh at me.
On the full moon of the first month of the Renyin year, I now explain this text. It consists briefly of forty-four chapters:
[1] One Hundred Dharmas; [2] Meaning of Delusion regarding the Truths; [3] Meaning of Subduing and Severing in the Mahāyāna.

The meaning of the subduing and abandoning [of afflictions] in the Hīnayāna; the meaning of the subduing and abandoning [of afflictions] in the Pratyekabuddhayāna; the meaning of the provisions and application stages in the Mahāyāna; the meaning of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); the meaning of the characteristics of the path of seeing; the meaning of the conditions for the path of seeing;

the two masters’ fourteen and eleven interpretations regarding the simultaneous and gradual abandonment [of afflictions]; and the meaning of the established truths (*satya*) within the path of seeing.
The meaning of the six clear realizations; the meaning of the path of cultivation; the meaning of the exposition of the ten stages;
the meaning of the ten superior practices; the meaning of the ten heavy obstacles; the meaning of the ten suchnesses;
the meaning of the transformation of the basis; the meaning of the four nirvāṇas; and the meaning of the four wisdoms.
The meaning of the three objects; the provisional meaning of self and dharmas; the twenty-seven noble meanings;
the meaning of manifest and unmanifest [karma]; the analysis through questions and answers; the meaning of specific and general characteristics;
the six meanings of seeds; the meaning of residual fruits; and the meaning of the perfuming of new [seeds].
The meaning of the fourfold division, the meaning of delusion regarding a stump, the meaning of the four types of karma,
the meaning of the cessation of perception and feeling, the meaning of the five fruits, the meaning of causal conditions,
the meaning of immediate conditions, the meaning of object conditions, and the meaning of dominant conditions.
The ten causes; the fifteen meanings of the basis; the meaning of merit and demerit; the eight meanings of liberation;
the meaning of the link of name-and-form; the distinction between the twelve links of existence and the outflows;
and the two types of birth and death.

The meaning of the one hundred dharmas is solely to negate external objects apart from the mind. By distinguishing the aspects transformed by the seeing-consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*), it indicates that the mind is not empty;

thus, five categories are taught, totaling one hundred dharmas. First, the eight [dharmas] existing by way of self-nature (*svabhāva*) are: first, eye-consciousness; second, ear-consciousness; third, nose-consciousness; fourth, tongue-consciousness; fifth...
The body; the six mental factors; the seven faculties; the eight resultant [factors]; the fifty-one associated [factors]:

five universal, five object-specific, eleven wholesome, twenty-six root and secondary afflictions, and four indeterminate; the eleven states of the three [times]; form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental objects;
the five physical sense organs of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body; the twenty-four distinctions of the four [types of] acquisition; and first, attainment. Second...

1. The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). 2. The homogeneity of the three groups (*nikāyasabhāga*). 3. The nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*). 4. The attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*). There are six [factors] existing as substantial entities (*dravyasat*):

1. Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*). 2. Cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*). 3. The cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha*). 4. The immovable (*āniñjya*). 5. Space (*ākāśa*). 6. Suchness (*tathatā*).

The nature of consciousness refers to the first five consciousnesses, which are permeated by the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate. They take only present direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as their object and cause. The sixth [consciousness] also possesses spontaneous conceptualization (*svarasavāhin-vikalpa*).

It is associated with thirty-one mental factors (*caitta*) and perfumes only the seeds of names and phrases (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-bīja*) within the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*). It is associated with...

The immediate retribution for one's parents consists of the six consciousnesses, which possess the three natures (wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral) and comprise both innate and discriminative [cognition]. They take as their objects the three types of valid cognition—perception, inference, and non-perceptual testimony—and they bring about both collective and individual retributions.
They are accompanied by fifty-one mental factors and perfume the seeds of the seeing and appearing portions. A single moment of wholesome or unwholesome karma [is thus established].
The aggregate of maturation is the dominant condition.
The seventh manas-consciousness is of the nature of obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta). It takes only non-valid cognition as its object, grasping the eighth consciousness as a self.
Eighteen mental factors (caitta) continue without interruption; two types of grasping arise constantly, perfuming the seeds of the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) and the image-part (nimitta-bhāga).

The specific dominant condition (*viśeṣādhipati-pratyaya*) is the eighth consciousness, the ālayavijñāna. It is of an unobscured-neutral nature (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), accompanied by the five universal mental factors (*sarvatraga-caitta*). It takes as its objects only present direct perception (*pratyakṣa*):

seeds, the sense organs (*indriya*), the body, and the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*). Although it contains both contaminated and uncontaminated seeds, these are not afflictions; rather, they constitute the substance of retribution (*vipāka*).

The preceding maturation ceases and the subsequent maturation arises. There are four types of neutral (*avyākṛta*) states: first, deportment (*airyāpathika*); second, craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*);

third, transformation (*nairmāṇika*); and fourth, maturation (*vipākaja*). The first three are neutral and perfume seeds for names and words (*nāma-vyañjana-bīja*); the fourth is neutral and inferior.
The eighth consciousness in its entirety, and the first six consciousnesses in part, merely repay prior causes from previous lives and do not further perfume seeds.

That which is associated with consciousness always arises in dependence upon the mind; it is associated with the mind and bound to the mind. Its mode of activity consists in apprehending objects; its essence and all its external functions are manifest.
There are five universal mental factors that pervade the eight consciousnesses, the three natures, the three realms, and the three periods of time.

Whether contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), contact (*sparśa*) is one. It is defined as the differentiation and transformation resulting from the conjunction of the three, having the nature of causing the mind and mental factors to encounter their objects, and functioning as the basis for feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and so forth.
When the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness mutually accord with one another, contact arises in dependence upon them.
Causing them to harmonize and function as mutual causes and effects, the functional capacity that gives rise to mental factors in accordance with this is called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*).
Contact arises resembling that [transformation] and is thus called "discrimination" (*vikalpa*).

The two types of attention (*manasikāra*) are the activity of the mind; their nature is to alert the mind, and they function toward that which is to arise, or they act in concert with the manifest consciousness.
At that time, its function is to draw the mind toward the focal object (*ālambana*). It alerts the mind and mental factors, causing them to move toward the preceding object.

The three types of sensation (*vedanā*) have the nature of experiencing (*anubhava*) and the function of giving rise to craving (*tṛṣṇā*). However, "sensation of the object" (*viṣaya-vedanā*) is not common to other dharmas;
it refers specifically to that which belongs to oneself regarding objects that are either adverse, favorable, or neutral. This is termed the "sensation of the object."
The four perceptions have the grasping of images as their intrinsic nature and the establishment of various names and conventions as their function.
Because they grasp objective spheres of common characteristics—such as blue, yellow, and so forth—from the perspective of both cause and effect, they give rise to verbal expression.
The five volitions (cetanā) have the nature of causing the mind to engage in activity. Their function is to employ the mind with respect to wholesome or unwholesome objects.

They are neither exclusively correct causes nor exclusively false causes; rather, their characteristic is that they serve as the causes for the production of bodily and vocal actions. There are three [types] because there are three [kinds of] objects.

There are five object-determining mental factors (*viṣaya-viniyata*), which arise in relation to four types of objects: first, that which is desired; second, that which is determined; third, that which has been previously experienced; fourth, that which is being observed; and fifth, that which is being contemplated.
All of these have objective referents (*ālambana*) consisting of entities or events. For the most part, they differ from one another and do not necessarily arise simultaneously.

First is desire (*chanda*). Regarding objects that are desired, for one who wishes to investigate them, desire arises; it ceases spontaneously when [the object] is no longer present. Its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is aspiration;

its function (*karman*) is to serve as the basis for diligence (*vīrya*). Diligence pertains to all three moral natures (*trividha-svabhāva*): diligence toward the unwholesome (*akuśala*) is itself laziness (*kausīdya*);
diligence toward the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) is itself resolve (*adhimokṣa*); and diligence toward the wholesome (*kuśala*) is itself vigor (*vīrya*). As for the objects...
There are three types of resolve (*adhimokṣa*): first, that which is desired; second, that which is sought; and third, that which is investigated.
Secondly, there is the resolve as a mental factor (*caitasika*), which has the nature of confirming and maintaining a determined object, and its function is to be unshakeable.
It confirms teachings that are false, correct, or neither, and even when other conditions arise, it cannot be diverted. This applies to objects regarding which one might otherwise have doubt.
It is simply non-existent.

The three types of mindfulness have as their nature causing the mind to clearly remember objects previously experienced, and as their function, serving as the basis for meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Regarding their essence (*svabhāva*) and their objects (*ālambana*), one should distinguish four permutations: first, a defiled mind taking the aggregate of suffering as its object; this is an "object of the same category" (*jātisama*) for the essence [of mindfulness]. Second, a defiled...

1. The mind that takes uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) names as its object is a category of name. 2. The three [moments of] the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) that realize the essence of suchness (*tathatā*) is a category of name.
3. The uncontaminated mind that takes the names of suffering (*duḥkha*) and origination (*samudaya*) as its object is a category of essence.

The first five [consciousnesses] and the eighth [storehouse consciousness] are not termed "cognizing objects" (*ālambana*) because they do not involve generic observation; since these are not objects previously experienced, no mental attention (*manasikāra*) arises toward them.
The four concentrations (*dhyāna*) have the nature of causing the mind to focus intently on the object of observation without distraction, and their function is to serve as the basis for wisdom.
Regarding the discerning wisdom that operates within the spheres of gain, loss, and neutrality, it generates a state of mental focus. This does not imply that there is only a single object.
In the sixteen moments of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), there should be no arising of concentration (*samādhi*). If one is not focused single-mindedly, concentration does not arise;
therefore, [concentration] is not a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*).

The five types of wisdom (*prajñā*) have the nature of discerning their respective objects of observation, and their function is to sever doubt. They operate with respect to what is beneficial, what is harmful, and that which is neither.
The wisdom that investigates within its object does not exist in a state of delusion where there is no discernment; therefore, it is not universal.
These five arise in relation to four types of objects and do not necessarily arise together. One should explain these five as arising individually:
when the subject and object are observed separately, concentration and wisdom arise individually regarding the object of observation alone, in order to suppress distraction.
The mind does not exercise discernment; there is concentration but no wisdom, as in the case of the gods who forget through play.
Or, one does not focus intently on the object of observation while investigating the characteristics of phenomena; there is wisdom but no concentration.
The examination of these various categories consists of eleven points:

first, listing the names; second, identifying their essential nature (*svabhāva*); third, their function (*karman*); fourth, whether they exist within the eight consciousnesses; and fifth, the various interpretations.

Regarding the first point, some maintain that the five sensory consciousnesses lack this self-nature because they are distracted and incapable of deliberation. Others maintain that the five sensory consciousnesses may possess it, even though they lack [deliberative] thought.
Regarding the predominant mental factors (*adhipati-caitta*) and the object-specific ones (*viṣaya-viniyata-caitta*):

even when desire (*chanda*) is weak or inferior, and one has not yet attained mastery, these five are entirely absent in the eighth consciousness, while they are partially present in the sixth and seventh. When mastery is attained from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onward, these five are definitely present in all eight types of consciousness, just like the five universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*).

Regarding the five [faculties] associated with the five feelings: one interpretation holds that they exclude pleasure (*sukha*) and desire (*chanda*), while excluding sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and pain (*duḥkha*); the other four are associated with three feelings.

Another interpretation holds that they are associated with all five feelings. The treatise states that the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) consists of longing for, grieving over, and being distressed by the unsurpassed Dharma.
Because they seek to realize [the truth], and because they seek liberation from the realm of superficial suffering, these five [factors] further depend upon six categories:

the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the three trainings (*triśikṣā*), the three types of abandonment (*trihāna*), and the outflowing (*sāsrava*) versus non-outflowing (*anāsrava*), as well as retribution (*vipāka*) versus non-retribution.
Whether they coexist with afflictions (*kleśa*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), or virtuous minds (*kuśalacitta*), and whether they are concomitant or not, shall be understood in detail below.

The eleven wholesome [mental factors] are those that arise exclusively in association with a wholesome mind; they are called wholesome mental concomitants (*caitta*). These consist of faith, shame, and so forth.
There are definitely eleven, which are subsumed into eight:

first is faith (*śraddhā*), which has the nature of a clear and pure mind characterized by deep conviction and aspiration toward reality, virtue, and capability (the cause), and its fruit. It is the antidote to...
Its function is to counteract lack of faith. Its intrinsic nature is clarity and purity; it is able to purify other mental factors (*caitta*). This is the specific characteristic of faith.

In terms of its substantial reality (*dravya*), it permeates all three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Substantially, it brings about future retribution. Among all phenomena—whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*)—it is exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*) among their qualities.

There are six aspects of the Three Jewels (*triratna*): first, the representative forms: the Buddha represented by clay or painted images, the Dharma represented by the yellow scrolls [of scripture], and the Sangha represented by those clad in dyed robes. Second...

The Hīnayāna; the six-foot Buddha; the Dharma of the Āgamas; the Sangha of the four fruits; those prior to the third bhūmi; the thousand-foot Buddha; the Dharma of the stages of abiding, practice, and orientation;
the Sangha of the three types of noble ones; those from the fourth bhūmi upward; the ten levels of the other-enjoyment Buddha; the Dharma of the progressive increase of the ten pāramitās;
the Sangha of the bodhisattvas of the ten bhūmis; the fifth stage of equal enlightenment; the reward-body Buddha; the perfectly integrated Dharma; and the one in the position of succession.
The Saṃgha of those who have attained birth once more; the six types of one-pointedness of mind; the Buddha as Awakened Illumination;

the Dharma as the Sustaining Track; and the Saṃgha as Non-contention. These two—shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*)—are explained together. To revere and honor the noble and good is the specific characteristic of shame. To despise and reject the violent and evil is the specific characteristic of dread of blame.
Shame arises through the power of the Noble Teaching as its condition; dread of blame arises through the power of the world as its condition. Regarding the noble person...
Wholesome phenomena manifest the condition for *hrī* (self-respect), while unwholesome persons and unwholesome phenomena manifest the condition for *apatrāpya* (dread of blame).

To feel shame regarding transgressions and faults is the common characteristic of these two. These two do not necessarily coexist; depending on the circumstances and the object, their intensity varies.
Even within a pure land, *apatrāpya* can arise.

Regarding the three roots, non-attachment and so forth: why are they called "roots"? Because they are preeminent in producing the wholesome and because they act as antidotes to the unwholesome, they are termed "wholesome roots.

Non-attachment has as its nature being untainted toward existence (*bhava*) and the requisites of existence—the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the three realms—and it acts as the antidote to attachment.

Non-hatred (*adveṣa*) has the nature of being free from malice toward suffering and the instruments of suffering— the three realms and the five aggregates— and its function is the production of wholesome states.

Non-delusion (*amoha*) has the nature of being free from darkness regarding all principles and phenomena, possesses a distinct intrinsic nature, and its function is the production of wholesome states.
The four right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*). Their nature is vigor (*vīrya*) characterized by courage and resistance. Courage is not a defiled dharma, and resistance is not indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
They arise after the three roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) and function as the antidote to laziness (*kausīdya*).

Fifth is pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). Some say that it exists throughout the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and that there is also a state of flexibility (*praśrabdhi*) induced by meditative concentration (*samādhi*) within wholesome minds (*kuśalacitta*).

Others say that pliancy does not exist in the desire realm and is not pervasive across all wholesome minds; it exists only in the stages of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*), having functional adaptability as its nature and serving as the antidote to lethargy (*styāna*).

The six forms of non-negligence (*apramāda*) take as their essence the four dharmas of non-attachment (*alobha*), diligence (*vīrya*), and so forth. Their nature consists of guarding and cultivating the objects of practice.
Although faith, shame (*hrī*), and other such qualities also possess this capacity, they do not serve as its primary basis.

Seventh is equanimity. Within mindfulness, one abides in balance and uprightness. Through heedfulness, having first removed all defilements, one practices equanimity to cause the mind to dwell in purity, thereby counteracting restlessness.
The eighth is non-harming (*avihiṃsā*). Its intrinsic nature is not to afflict sentient beings. Non-harming is a designation based on a portion of non-hatred (*adveṣa*), which exists substantially.

Non-hatred consists in bestowing happiness, while non-harming consists in extracting suffering; this is in order to manifest the distinct characteristics of these two, namely compassion (*karuṇā*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
The examination of these various gates consists of twelve parts:

first, listing the names; second, defining their essential nature as in the text; third, answering the question of whether it is better to be pure with few defilements or otherwise, by stating "according to reality," etc., based on the differences between delusion and awakening, and between the universal and the specific;
fourth, the functions of the three karmas; fifth, the three provisional designations; sixth, [the section on] non-negligence, which abandons indolence.

[The first] is harmful. The remaining eight are substantially existent. Five arise simultaneously with their own kind. Some say: among the eleven [mental factors], four are universal to wholesome minds—namely, faith (*śraddhā*) and the three roots;
the remaining seven are non-universal. Others say: ten are universal to wholesome minds. [The factor of] pliancy acquired through maturation exists in the meditative stages (*samāhitabhūmi*);
six [of the eleven] exist there. The presence or absence of the eight consciousnesses varies according to the stage; the first six are certain.

1. All stages possess [these factors], though *praśrabdhi* (serenity) is occasionally absent. 2. The seventh and eighth [consciousnesses] have no cause but possess the fruit, because they lack the causes [of the preceding moments]. 3.

Seventy dharmas coexist with the five types of sensation (*vedanā*), excluding the sensations of sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and suffering (*duḥkha*), because they pervade all three realms. 4. These ten [factors] are not incompatible with the universal (*sarvatraga*) or object-specific (*viṣayaviniyata*) mental factors, as they can arise simultaneously with them;
furthermore, they pervade both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*). 5. These thirteen [factors] are of a determinate nature (*niyata-svabhāva*).
10. Among these, only the wholesome [factors] exist. 11. These ten, excluding *praśrabdhi* (serenity), exist throughout all three realms.
12. These eleven are not abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*);

those that are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) are impure wholesome states, while those that are not to be abandoned are the inferior untainted states. [This refers to] faith and the others.
The Five Faculties.
Regarding the inversion of their defiled and purified aspects, the verse says:
The aspects of activity are inverted as equanimity, pride, and dejection; Doubt and views are the three great natures that serve as antidotes.
Among the three great and four small faculties, whichever is present is collectively termed "defiled" or "pure" based on their mutual opposition.

If this mental factor opposes that factor in its mode of activity (*ākāra*), it is a reversal of the mode of activity. If it opposes that factor in its essential substance (*svabhāva*), it is a reversal of both the substance and the mode of activity.
If it pervades all three natures and is mixed with the wholesome and the defiled, it is categorized as belonging to the nature of the "object-specific" (*viṣayapratiniyataviṣaya*) factors.
The nature of wholesome wisdom (*kuśala-prajñā*) serves as the antidote to defiled wisdom (*kliṣṭa-prajñā*). Regarding the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), there are six;

however, various treatises employ different terminology for them, resulting in three interpretations. First, in the *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra*, following the two views associated with doubt, it refers specifically to those that are purely conceptual (*vikalpika*);
this implies that the innate (*sahaja*) and conceptual types are treated as preceding them. Second, in the *Dvayaśata-dharma-śāstra*, ignorance (*avidyā*) is placed before pride (*māna*).
Regarding the sequence: those [afflictions] common to both the sharp and dull faculties are placed first;

the five views and doubt delude only through the sharp faculty regarding principles (*tattva*), whereas greed, hatred, and pride delude through both the sharp and dull faculties regarding both phenomena (*dharma*) and principles. According to the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, these three are listed before the roots of unwholesomeness;
thus, pride is not a root of unwholesomeness and is placed after ignorance (*avidyā*).
First is greed (*rāga*), which has the nature of being stained by attachment toward existence and the requisites for existence.
Second is hatred (*dveṣa*), which has the nature of increasing malice toward suffering and the requisites for suffering.
Third is delusion (*moha*), which has the nature of confusion and darkness regarding all principles and phenomena. The function of these three is that they are all capable of producing suffering.
The four types of pride (*māna*) have the nature of exalting oneself in relation to others based on self-reliance; their function is to obstruct non-pride and to give rise to suffering.
Because one’s mind does not become humble toward those who possess virtue or are virtuous, one revolves in saṃsāra and undergoes suffering.

Thus, there are seven entities and nine categories. Regarding three grades of objects, three grades of mental states arise: when [the object] is superior, inferior, or equal, they are distinguished as high, low, and middle, respectively. As for the former...

Regarding the four types of pride (*māna*): the first arises by taking external objects as its objective condition and giving rise to the view of "other" and "self"; this is the pride of disparagement (*abhimāna*).

The latter three take internal objects as their objective condition and give rise to the pride of relying upon oneself; because they do not constitute distinct categories of phenomena (*dharma-saṃkhyā*), they are not established as separate types.

As for the seven entities: the first is simple pride (*māna*), which, regarding inferior objects, conceives of oneself as superior; regarding middling objects, it conceives of oneself as equal... [and so forth].

1. *Māna* (pride): regarding an object of middling quality, one gives rise to the conceit that one is equal [to others who are superior]. 2. *Abhimāna* (excessive pride): regarding an object of superior quality, one gives rise to the conceit that one is equal [to those who are superior].
3. *Mānātimāna* (pride beyond pride): regarding only an object of superior quality, one gives rise to the conceit that one is superior [to those who are superior].
4. *Ūnamāna* (inferiority pride): arising only regarding an object of superior quality, one considers oneself inferior. 5. *Adhimāna* (overweening pride): taking what is little as much.
Sixth is the pride of self (asmimāna), which conceives the aggregates as a self. Seventh is false pride (mithyāmāna), which regards what is entirely non-existent as existent.

Regarding the nine types [of pride]: "I am superior" (the pride of overestimation); "I am equal" (pride); "I am inferior" (the pride of inferiority). "There is one superior to me" (the pride of overestimation); "There is one equal to me" (pride);

"There is one inferior to me" (the pride of overestimation). "There is no one superior to me" (pride); "There is no one inferior to me" (the pride of inferiority); "There is no one equal to me" (the pride of overestimation). These first three categories [are as follows].
Comparing oneself with others constitutes the latter six types [of pride]. Comparing others with oneself has the meaning of affirmation; the absence of such comparison has the meaning of negation.
Regarding the object of perception (*ālambana*) being superior while the perceiving mind is inferior, the *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya* states:
"Six arise from superiority; three arise from inferiority-pride (*ūnamāna*): 'I am inferior,' 'I have excellence,' and 'I do not have inferiority. If one relies on the *Prakaraṇapāda*, [it says]:...

The treatise [states]: Three arise based on one grade; for instance, thinking "I am superior," "there are those inferior to me," or "there are none equal to me," all of which belong to the category of *abhimāna* (overweening pride).
Three arise based on three grades; for instance, thinking "I am equal," "there are those inferior to me," or "there are none inferior to me. One arises based on three grades and one grade;

for instance, thinking "I am superior," "there are those inferior to me," or "there are none inferior to me"—all of which belong to the category of *ūnamāna* (inferiority pride). Thus, this root treatise is for the most part not the same as the *Pāda-śāstra*.
Furthermore, there is another fault:
the five types of doubt (*vicikitsā*). Its intrinsic nature is hesitation regarding various principles and phenomena; it functions to obstruct the absence of doubt.

It gives rise to doubt concerning the causes and effects of future lives, the Three Jewels, and the Four Noble Truths. Although its characteristic is to take both principles and phenomena as its objects, it is a delusion regarding principle alone, and not [a delusion regarding phenomena].
Like the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*), these take only phenomena as their object and are deluded regarding phenomena.

The six views of self-identity (*sat-kāya-dṛṣṭi*) have defiled wisdom as their nature; they function through discrimination by taking the aggregates (*skandha*) as their object, yet do not discriminate the specific basis from which they arise.

Fourth is the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*). Relying upon the concentration of immediate succession (*ānantarya-samādhi*), it gives rise to the highest degree of knowledge that accords with reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).

In a single moment, it simultaneously seals both the emptiness of the previously mentioned subject and object; thus it is called the "Supreme Mundane. As it is the final thought-moment within the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*), immediately following the contaminated (*sāsrava*) state, the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) arises.

Since there is no uncontaminated [state] existing [prior to this], the contaminated does not arise. Given that there is no real object, one is free from the grasping consciousness (*grāhaka-vijñāna*).

There is indeed a real consciousness that, being separated from the objects of apprehension, gives rise to wisdom as it truly is—free from outflows—and wherein both the grasping at self and phenomena are absent;

therefore, it is called the "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*). If one enters the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), it occurs solely by relying on a body of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and a mind of the fourth dhyāna.

The other two types of revulsion are not particularly distinguished; therefore, the stages of *ūṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, and *kṣānti* may all rely upon any of the first three dhyānas or the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).
However, the *laukikāgra-dharma* relies exclusively on the mind of the fourth dhyāna. As for the four roots of merit (*kuśala-mūla*) of the two vehicles (*yāna*), [the same applies].

Relying solely on the first dhyāna, one turns the mind toward the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya*) and enters the Mahāyāna path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Therein, one abandons only the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), and it is maintained that entry occurs while relying on a body belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Regarding the meaning of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*): when there is no apprehension whatsoever of an object within cognition, at that time one abides in consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), free from the characteristics of the grasped and the grasper.

Thus, the mind and its object correspond, like the merging of wisdom with its object; free from the two graspings, conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is cut off. There are three types of the realizing wisdom.

First, it is said that both the objective aspect (*nimitta*) and the subjective aspect (*darśana*) are non-existent, and thus there is no duality of grasped and grasper. Second, it is said that both parts exist;

for if there were no objective aspect to serve as the object of perception, one would have to conclude that sound is not seen, and that the subjective aspect is not a cognitive faculty (*ālambaka*). Third, it is said that the objective aspect exists while the subjective aspect is non-existent; this refers to non-conceptual vision.

Here, the subjective aspect is narrow in scope and carries the essence and characteristics of *tathatā* (suchness). When the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*) arises, untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is produced. The realization of the essence of *tathatā* is called [the stage of] "seeing" (*darśana*).

It constitutes the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*). Because it first illuminates the principle, it gives rise to great joy. The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "In reality, it abandons the two obstacles;

it truly realizes the true principle revealed by the two kinds of emptiness regarding the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of conceptual construction. Although this process involves many moments (*kṣaṇa*) before reaching its ultimate conclusion, because their characteristics are identical, they are collectively termed 'one mind'."

The Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*) consists of the subsequent non-contaminated wisdom (*anāsrava-prsthalabdha-jñāna*) that takes the non-established [truth] as its object. Its seeing aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) perceives the principle of true vision and emulates it by generating three moments of mind:

first, the wisdom that internally negates the existence of intrinsic nature, which eliminates the afflictions of the lower grade of the two obscurations; second, the wisdom that externally negates the conventional designation of all phenomena, which eliminates the cognitive obscurations.

Grasping at the middle grade of afflictions, one universally dispels the three types of conventional cognition regarding the internal and external, thereby eliminating the two superior grades of the obstacles.

If following the model of the Hīnayāna, both are considered afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*). If following the model of the Mahāyāna, all phenomena pertaining to sentient beings constitute the two obstacles;

the coarse ones are divided into two, while the subtle ones constitute one. The third stage follows the realization. The first two minds differ in their general and specific aspects, as well as in the names of the objects they take; [the object of] phenomena...

Collectively, they take names and categories as their objects. Regarding the three objects, those below are called "dharma-objects" (dharmālambana) and those above are called "category-objects" (jātyālambana).
If one separately emulates [the function of] two paths of uninterrupted transition (ānantaryamārga), one collectively emulates one path of liberation (vimuktimārga).

Regarding the statement that the fourteen [moments] of liberation are gradually severed: herein, the two types of emptiness and the two types of hindrances are gradually severed and gradually realized. This is because there are differences in the depth of their underlying principles and the coarseness or subtlety of the hindrances.

Each of the two types of hindrances is divided into three grades; by severing them in succession, six moments of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya*) and six moments of liberation (*vimukti*) are produced.

1. Liberation (*vimokṣa*). 2. Superior progress (*viśeṣagamana*). Together, these constitute fourteen moments of mind. 3. When employing thirteen moments of mind—excluding the intermediate superior progress.

4. When employing twelve moments of mind—excluding the final superior progress. 5. If one employs the subsequent uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), then there are eight moments of mind for the preceding liberation:
six uninterrupted paths, one liberation, and one superior progress. 6. When employing seven moments of mind—excluding the final superior progress. 6. [End of section].

The two obstructions are each divided into two categories. There are five moments of mind: four uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*), four paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and two paths of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*).

[Specifically: seven exclude the final path of superior progress; eight exclude the intermediate paths of superior progress; nine employ the subsequent uninterrupted path which is identical to the preceding path of liberation. Thus, there are five moments of mind.
10. Excluding the final *viśeṣa-bhāgīya*, there are eleven moments; the coarse aspects of the two obstacles are abandoned separately, while the subtle aspects are abandoned together in seven moments.
11. Excluding the final *viśeṣa-bhāgīya*, there are six moments. 12. In the subsequent immediate [moment], which is identical to the preceding liberation, there are four moments.
13. Excluding the final *viśeṣa-bhāgīya*, there are three moments.

Regarding the statement that the eleven [categories of] afflictions are severed instantaneously, some say: herein, the two emptinesses and the two obstacles are severed and realized simultaneously by means of the true path of seeing (*tattva-darśana-mārga*), because it does not take [them] as distinct objects.

Thus, the two obstacles are combined into two great categories, employing three paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and three paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), along with one path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*). This constitutes seven moments of mind, excluding [the final moment].

Regarding the final *viśeṣa-mārga* (path of excellence): if the six minds follow immediately [after the preceding], they are the same as the preceding *vimukti-mārga* (paths of liberation). Regarding the four minds—excluding the final *viśeṣa-mārga*—there are three minds;
if the coarse and subtle aspects of the two obstacles are both abandoned in two grades, there are two *anantarya-mārgas* (paths of uninterrupted transition) and two *vimukti-mārgas*.

Regarding the one *viśeṣa-mārga*—excluding the final *viśeṣa-mārga*—there are four minds following it; the immediate [successor] is the same as the preceding *vimukti-mārga*. There are three minds excluding the *viśeṣa-mārga*.
Progression involves two types of mind. If the two obstacles are combined into one great category, they may consist of three, two, or one.

In the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*), the uncontaminated subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) based on the established truths (*vyavasthāna-satya*) takes the aspectual division (*darśana-bhāga*) as its object; it constructs sixteen mental images (*citta-pratibimba*) that emulate true vision.
The path consists of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), which are divided with respect to the four truths.

In the lower stages, one abandons the delusions and realizes the principle. The seeing portion (*darśana-bhāga*) takes true suchness (*tathatā*) as its object; at that time, it abandons the delusions belonging to the four truths and realizes the principles belonging to the four truths. There are eight instances of this seeing portion.

As for its self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*), it realizes the four obstacles previously abandoned and the four principles realized; it takes the correct wisdom of contemplation (*bhāvanā-samyag-jñāna*) as its object. Now...

The Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*). This refers to the seeing aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), which resembles the abandonment and realization achieved within that true Path of Vision; hence it is said.

According to the *Abhidharmasamaya-prakaraṇa-śāstra*: "The Dharma-patience and Dharma-knowledge regarding the Four Truths" (the seeing aspect is so named by its intrinsic nature as it abandons delusions)—this serves to abandon the twenty-eight types of conceptual proclivities (*vikalpa-anuśaya*) of the three realms (interpretation according to the *Abhidharmasamaya*).

"The Subsequent Knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) regarding the Four Truths" (the seeing aspect is so named for its realization of principle)—this realizes what was previously abandoned (interpretation according to the *Abhidharmasamaya*).

The *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti* (receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering) and so forth: [these] are established by name according to their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), being self-realized and realizing abandonment. Regarding the preceding *dharma-kṣāntis*, each is individually internally realized.

[These] are established by name by following the analogy of the *dharma* [kṣāntis] to understand their meaning. The four *anvaya-jñānas* (subsequent knowledges): [these] are established by name according to their intrinsic nature, being self-realized and realizing the object; they realize the principle through the aspect of vision (*darśana-bhāga*). They confirm the preceding confirmations.

Furthermore, regarding the objects of the higher and lower truths, one does not speak of the self-realized aspect (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*) but discusses only the aspect of vision. That which is present before one in the lower realm is called "dharma" (*dharma*); that which is not present before one in the upper [realms] is called "subsequent" (*anvaya*).

Regarding the two realms, these categories comprise the three realms. Below the Four Noble Truths, there are one hundred and twelve types of conceptual differentiation. The *Treatise on Afflictions* states:

"In the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), both the uninterrupted (*ānantarya*) and the liberation (*vimukti*) stages each possess the self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) as established through their specific distinctions."

The meaning of the six types of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) is as follows: 1. **Clear realization through reflection**: This is wisdom associated with intense feelings of joy that reflects upon objects characterized by common features (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).

2. **Clear realization accompanied by faith**: This consists of the four unshakable faiths (*aveṇika-śraddhā*). 3. **Clear realization of morality**: Because it assists in the accomplishment of wisdom. 4. **Clear realization of wisdom**: This is wisdom itself.

The truth of wisdom; the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of that truth; the limit of the five clear realizations; namely, the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) regarding the truth of the wisdom of wisdom;

and the sixth, the ultimate, which is the clear realization itself. The former [six] are the specific names for the latter clear realization, while their general name is the "True Path of Seeing" (*darśana-mārga*).

This includes everything from the untainted precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*) up to the ultimate stage, and is subsumed under a small portion of the "Path of Seeing with Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-darśana-mārga*).
The fifth [type of clear realization] is complete; the remaining four are partial, excluding the fourth clear realization.

The verse says: This one does not rely on meditative absorption (dhyāna). (The clear realization through reflection does not rely on the concentrations of the nine stages. Three rely on five bases for their arising. (The latter three arise in the threshold concentration [anāgamya] and the fundamental states of the four dhyānas.

One type is likewise partial. (This refers to the clear realization through faith. The remainder rely on all bases. (The clear realization through morality does not rely on the concentrations of the nine stages.)

The meaning of the path of cultivation is non-attainment and inconceivable; it is supramundane wisdom. Because it abandons the two types of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*), one thereby realizes the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).

The first two phrases are devoid of subject and object; they constitute fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). The latter two phrases pertain to the meaning of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), which takes subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) as its basis.

The term "basis" (*āśraya*) applies to both the defiled and the pure; here, the transformation of the word "basis" serves as the cause. By abandoning the defiled and attaining the pure, this is the basis of transformation, namely, untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
Regarding the seeds, there are originally three grades. Furthermore, the newly perfumed seeds likewise consist of three kinds of wisdom-essence. This constitutes one transformation.

It eliminates the inferior [defilements] and serves to support the new cultivation of the lower grade; it equals the innate middle grade and supports the new cultivation of the middle grade; and it equals the innate superior grade.

When a single moment of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) arises, its functions are threefold: first, it supports the new cultivation of the superior grade; second, it incidentally supports the myriad practices (*sādhana*);
and third, it functions from below to increase [the roots of goodness]. It is not said that there are delusions to be severed within untainted wisdom; rather, it simply opposes them.

The two obstacles (āvaraṇa) are rendered such that their seeds and essences never arise again. Regarding the functional capacities for both defilement and purification, the nature of ordinary beings (pṛthagjanatva) is established as superior; the nature of the noble ones (āryatva) is subsumed under the category of non-associated [formations] (viprayukta-saṃskāra).
This is explained in the *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya*.
1. The ultimate is joy; 2. the departure from defilement; 3. the manifestation of light; 4. wisdom like a flame; 5. victory over difficulties;
6. the immediate presence; 7. the far-reaching practice; 8. the immovability; 9. the wisdom of goodness; 10. the Dharma like a cloud.
Each stage (*bhūmi*) is explained in four ways: 1. If "the stage of Perfect Joy" (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), then "joy" (*prīti*) refers to the wisdom of preparatory application (*prayoga-jñāna*).

2. If "the stage that is Perfect Joy," then "joy" refers to the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). 3. If "the stage of Perfect Joy," using the specific term to distinguish it from the general, this refers to the practice within subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
4. If "Perfect Joy itself is the stage," this refers to the true suchness (*tathatā*) realized therein.

Regarding the meaning of the ten superior practices (*daśa-prakāra-viśeṣa*), there are three types of the first six practices as found in the *Abhidharma-kośa* (Treatise on Higher Knowledge), just as the six practices are grouped into three stages; their breadth and narrowness can thus be understood.
Each of the latter four has two types. There must be seven kinds of supremacy (*saptavidha-viśeṣa*) for the meaning of "crossing over" (*pāramitā*) to be established. First, peace (*kṣema*).

1. Abiding in the nature of enlightenment (*bodhigotra*); 2. relying upon the bodhicitta; 3. having the altruistic intention (*āśaya*) of compassion for sentient beings; 4. being complete in the performance of activities; 5.

possessing skillful means (*upāya*) and the wisdom of signlessness (*animittajñāna*); 6. dedicating [merit] toward unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttarabodhi*); and 7. not being hindered by the two obscurations (*āvaraṇa*).
These should be combined into four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*): 1. That which is giving but not a perfection (*pāramitā*), lacking the seven excellences (*saptavidha-prakāra*). 2.

That which is a perfection but not giving, such as sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), which possesses the seven excellences. 3. That which is both a perfection and giving, as should be understood. 4. That which is neither, such as [giving] characterized by greed and so forth.

The first three—giving, ethical discipline, and patience—are the superior paths for increasing the status of humans and devas; the latter three—diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—constitute the definitive path to supreme victory (*abhisamaya*). These are the skillful means (*upāya*).

Generosity is assisted by morality, patience, aspiration, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. Regarding the general practice of these six perfections, a single act of giving invariably attains five fruits:
first, by severing stinginess, one attains the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*); second, by benefiting oneself and others, one attains the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*);

third, by obtaining an excellent place of rebirth, one attains the fruit of natural outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*); fourth, by leading toward great *nirvāṇa*, one attains the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*); and fifth, one experiences the acquisition of great wealth.
The fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).

The meaning of the ten heavy obstacles is the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*). They obstruct wholesome and unwholesome karma; these are the causes of maturation. The retribution of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) is the fruit of maturation. This is the fruit.

Arising from distinct causes is "differentiation. The five aggregates born of retribution possess a general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Among these, the defiled phenomena within the body are designated by names derived from their general basis;

this is the nature of arising. This nature consists of the two obstacles: the obstacle of the seeds themselves and the obstacle of the functional capacity upon those seeds. This is the obstacle to the nature.
When the seeds, which are the basis, are severed, the functional capacity, which depends upon them, can no longer arise; this is termed "noble nature" (*ārya-dhātu*).

However, both ignorance (*moha*) and coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) are the innate grasping at phenomena (*sahaja-dharma-grāha*) within the sixth consciousness; they are severed by means of the seven stages.

If an obstruction is itself ignorance, there are no afflictions (*kleśa*) within that obstruction. If it is the ignorance of an obstruction, this obstruction encompasses both types of obstructions (*dvaya-āvaraṇa*), taking a portion of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) as its essence.

First is the Ground of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), which abandons the obstruction of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*), the delusion of clinging to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-abhiniveśa-moha*), and the delusion of the defilement of the miserable realms (*apāya-saṃkleśa-moha*).

Second is the Ground of Purity (*vimalā-bhūmi*), which abandons the obstruction of wrong conduct (*mithyāpratipatti-āvaraṇa*), the delusion of subtle transgressions (*sūkṣma-āpatti-moha*), and the delusion of various miserable realms (*nānā-apāya-moha*).

Third is the Ground of Luminosity (*prabhākarī-bhūmi*). It severs the obscuration of dullness and ignorance, as well as the delusions of forgetfulness regarding what has been heard, reflected upon, and cultivated; the delusion of failing to retain what has been heard; and the four types of craving and greed.

Fourth is the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*). It severs the obscuration of active afflictions (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*). Previously, these [afflictions] frequently coexisted with the six consciousnesses that arise simultaneously with the cognitive objects (*jñeya-sahaja*);

now, the two innate views (*sahaja-dṛṣṭi*) never manifest again. Greed and hatred do not accompany them. Because these two views are associated with this [ground], they are termed "those whose companions have been destroyed" (*hatasahāya*).
There is delusion regarding meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and delusion regarding attachment to the Dharma.

In the fifth stage, the Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjaya*), one abandons the obstacles to parinirvāṇa of the lower vehicles, as well as delusion regarding turning one's back on saṃsāra and delusion regarding heading toward nirvāṇa.

Sixth, the Ground of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*): one abandons the obstruction of coarse signs and the delusions regarding the observation of cyclic existence (*pravṛtti*) and the manifestation of the signless (*animitta*).

Seventh, the Ground of Far-Going (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*): one abandons the delusion of subtle manifestations, the delusion regarding the flow of cyclic existence, and the delusion regarding arising and ceasing.

The eighth is the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*), which abandons the obstacle to unadulterated application (*anābhoga-prayoga-āvaraṇa*), the delusion regarding application (*prayoga-moha*), and the delusion regarding lack of mastery over signs and lands (*nimitta-kṣetra-vaśitā-moha*).

The ninth is the Ground of Good Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*), which abandons the obstacle to conduct that is not for one's own benefit (*svārtha-aprayoga-āvaraṇa*), the delusion regarding meaning and terminology (*artha-vyañjana-moha*), and the delusion regarding lack of mastery over eloquence (*pratibhāna-vaśitā-moha*).

The tenth is the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*). It eliminates the obstacle to attaining mastery, the delusion regarding great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and the awakening to the subtle delusions.
The eleventh [ground] eliminates the Buddha’s supreme obstacle—the delusion of attachment to the knowable (*jñeya*) and the delusion of subtle hindrances.

The meaning of the ten kinds of *tathatā* (suchness) is based on teachings that accord with suchness; based on those teachings, one discusses suchness, whereby the realization of *tathatā* becomes increasingly superior.

When the ultimate intent is expressed through its verbal designations, there are ten types: 1. Pervasive; 2. Supreme; 3. Superior Flow; 4. Without Appropriation; 5. No Distinction in Kind; 6. Untainted.
1. Purity; 2. the seven factors being without distinction; 3. non-increase and non-decrease; 4. mastery over knowledge; 5. mastery over karma.

Regarding the fruit of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) in terms of stages, there are six kinds of transformations: 1. Transformation through the weakening of power and the strengthening of capacity, which serves as confession;

by the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding the overcoming of faults and evils, the force of defiled seeds is weakened, while the functional capacity of pure seeds is strengthened. 2. Transformation through thorough penetration (*prativedha*). As for...
5. Transformation without inferiority; 6. Transformation of the perfection of the fruit.

Regarding the meaning of transformation (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), there is one [aspect] that is the path capable of transforming, which has two [subdivisions]: first, the path of subduing, which is the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*) where the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are subdued so that they do not arise, leading to...

Discriminating wisdom (*vikalpa-jñāna*). Second, the path capable of severing [afflictions]. On the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) severs the delusions regarding the principles and phenomena.

Second, there are two types of the basis that is transformed (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*): first, the basis that sustains seeds (*bīja-dhāra-āśraya*), which is the eighth consciousness (*aṣṭama-vijñāna*). It does not depend on others for the perfuming of defilement or purity.

This is pure and of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*). Second, the *tathatā* (suchness) is the basis for both delusion and awakening; it neither decreases in ordinary beings nor increases in the noble ones, remaining beyond defilement and purity.

Third, there are two types of relinquishment through transformation: first, relinquishment by abandonment, wherein the seeds of the obstacles are severed by the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) so that they never again manifest;

second, relinquishment by discarding, which consists of four things: first, contaminated virtue (*sāsrava-kuśala*); second, inferior uncontaminated states (*hīnānāsrava*); third, maturation (*vipāka*); [and fourth, the physical body].
[The nature of] the indeterminate is the four habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Within the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one abandons the inferior and attains the superior.

Regarding the four [types of] transformation, there are two kinds of attainment: first, that which is attained by birth, namely the mental states associated with the four wisdoms (*jñāna*), which comprise twenty-two dharmas;
second, that which is manifested through realization, the essence of *tathatā*. Because the three vehicles differ in their departure from obstructions, four types of nirvana are taught.
Through the perfuming and maintenance by the path of subduing, the seeds are supported; through the abandonment of that which is to be severed, one attains the enlightenment of the four wisdoms.
Through the realization of the path of severance, the basis of delusion and awakening is discarded. By the manifestation of these four matters, the four types of nirvāṇa are attained.
The four meanings of *nirvāṇa*:

first, the *nirvāṇa* of primordial purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa*), which all sentient beings possess in common; second, the *nirvāṇa with remainder* (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), which constitutes the three preceding fruits;

and third, the *nirvāṇa with remainder* wherein the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) are suppressed and severed through seven more rebirths, yet the wisdom of one who has attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) has not yet entered [the final state].

Cessation. There is the body which is the basis of suffering; in the nirvāṇa without remainder, those who delight in quiescence and the severance of ashes [attain] the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the Hīnayāna, while in the Mahāyāna, it is the true principle of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*).
This is the fourth, non-abiding nirvāṇa (*apratisthita-nirvāṇa*); because of compassion, one does not abide in nirvāṇa.
By virtue of wisdom, one does not abide in saṃsāra.

This distinguishes those in the three vehicles who are still in training (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*): they possess the first [perfection]. If those of indeterminate lineage (*aniyata-gotra*) turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle, they possess the first two and the fourth.
Those of the Mahāyāna who are still in training possess all three. As for those who dwell directly in the stages (*bhūmi*), they possess [all of them].
Regarding the beginning and the end: only the Buddha possesses all four. Why is this? The Buddha possesses *nirvāṇa with remainder*. Answer:

It is said metaphorically that the two vehicles attain only analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), yet they do not attain the basis of non-abiding. Why is this? Because they have severed the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) but have not attained [the ultimate] nirvāṇa.

Answer: The true principle of the emptiness of phenomena (dharmas) is that which has no abiding place. The first is the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) of suchness (tathatā); the latter three are the unconditioned of cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).

The immovable state of the cessation of perception and feeling (saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha) is subsumed under cessation not through deliberation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), while space (ākāśa) is comprised of the absence of obstruction.
The meaning of the four wisdoms:
First, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is itself wisdom; it can manifest and generate the reflections of bodies, lands, and wisdoms, which constitute the self-enjoyment body and its land.
Second, the Wisdom of the Equality of All Sentient Beings is established based on non-abiding nirvāṇa.
Established as a Bodhisattva of the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*), he manifests the body and land of the Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*).

Third, the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) observes both specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); its activity pervades the ten directions because it skillfully expounds the Dharma.

Fourth, the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Must Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*) manifests a body one thousand *zhang* tall for Bodhisattvas prior to the grounds, and a body sixteen *zhang* tall for ordinary beings, appearing in the forms of deer, horses, and so forth according to their kind. These four wisdoms are all...

There are thirty-two factors that collectively encompass all the merits of the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*). These transform the contaminated mental states associated with eight, seven, six, or five [factors].

Among these, the first five consciousnesses possess weak wisdom and superior discernment, while the sixth and seventh consciousnesses possess weak discernment and strong wisdom. Upon entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), they are transformed into wisdom.

It is only within the fruits of the eighth and the first five consciousnesses that these four types of mental states are finally transformed, taking all truths—both ultimate and conventional—as their objects.

Regarding the object (*viṣaya*): The treatise states, "This is the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*)" (explaining the name); "inconceivable, virtuous, and eternal" (praising its qualities); "the body of bliss and liberation."

The Great Muni is named Dharma (this distinguishes him from those at the stage of the cause and from the followers of the Two Vehicles). All outflows (*āsrava*) are forever exhausted (Arhats also possess this). Outflows do not increase therein (the first three fruits of the path also possess this).

His nature is pure (ordinary beings also possess this), and his clarity is perfected (those beyond training also possess this), as is his brilliance (Bodhisattvas also possess this). However, by reading the text more expansively, the scope of its meaning becomes far-reaching.
The Master Xuanzang’s Verses on the Meaning of the Three Objects: "The nature of the object of consciousness is good;

it does not follow the mind. A solitary image arises solely from the aspect (*darśana-bhāga*); An image with substance (*sadravya*) pertains to both the mental state and its objective basis, And includes the original nature, seeds, and so forth, according to their respective applications."

The single nature consists of five types of objects (*viṣaya*). These objects—whether sensory faculties (*indriya*) or external realms (*dhātu*)—arise from actual seeds and possess substantial entities and functions.

The cognizing mind attains their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), thereby abiding in its own nature rather than following the pervasive influence of the cognizer. Regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), there are two [types of] true natures;

the first is the "true object-nature" (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva-viṣaya*), which precedes the others. The five consciousnesses perceive the five sense-objects within their own realm; during the causal stage, they directly attain the essence of the eight consciousnesses respectively.

The self-witnessing division (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) takes the seeing division (*darśanabhāga*) as its object; these two are similar to real objects (*tattulyaviṣaya*). The sixth consciousness takes the mind of the preceding moment as its object, and it takes its own five sense organs as remote objects;
because they obtain their substance [only through representation], they are termed "similar" (*tulya*).

The second is the object with a shared substance (*sābhāsasadravya*). The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) manifests the image (*nimitta*), and the image carries the substance; this is the "carrying of the substance. That which carries it is the intermediate image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*).

When the image-part is subsumed back into its original substance, it is categorized solely as indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). However, when subsumed under the perceiving seeing-part, it may belong to any of the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*).

If one speaks of it separately from the seeing-part, it shares two characteristics with the original substance and its seeds: first, the "truly shared-substance" [object], which is perceived by the mind.

The mind possesses a real essence, as in the case of the seventh consciousness (*manas*), which takes the self-evident portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as its object and regards it as the intermediate aspect (*madhyamabhāga*) of the self;

in this case, the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) does not infuse seeds. Second, there is that which resembles the "aspect with substance" (*sadṛśasaviṣayabhāga*): when the minds of the first six consciousnesses take external objects as their objects, the intermediate objective aspect definitely infuses seeds; this is called "resembling the aspect with substance."

Third, the object of solitary reflection (*ekākāra-viṣaya*). The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the sixth consciousness transforms the objects of the three time periods; this is the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the independent mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). There are two types [of such images], both arising solely from the seeing-part:

first, those that possess substantial reality (*savastuka*), where the sixth consciousness perceives past and future phenomena. These include the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), their nature, their bonds, their seeds, and the three meditative attainments (*samāpatti*); these produce seeds of the image-part through simultaneous perfuming (*vāsana*), which subsequently arise.

Second, those without substantial reality (*avastuka*), where the sixth consciousness [perceives] the two non-existent entities. The sixth consciousness... [text ends] *(Note: The source text appears to be a fragment of a technical commentary on Yogācāra epistemology, specifically concerning the transformation of consciousness and the relationship between the seeing-part, the image-part, and the objects of the three time periods.)*

Taking as objects a real self and real dharmas through pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*), such as the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit, these do not perfume seeds and are subsumed under the category of pervasive conceptualization of form (*rūpa*).
Regarding the four natures and seeds, etc., "according to what is appropriate" means the sense of being indeterminate (*aniyata*). There are three combinations:

first, when the eighth [consciousness] takes objects of the scattered stage (*vikṣipta-bhūmi*) as its objects, the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) takes them as a real object (*svabhāva-viṣaya*), while the mental factors (*caitta*) take them as a solitary shadow (*chāyāmātra*). They do not perfume seeds. Second, the first five [consciousnesses]...
When the sense faculties and their objects of self and others serve as conditions, this is a "nature-object" (*svabhāva-viṣaya*); it also carries a substantial form (*sanimitta*) and perfumes seeds.

Third, when the sixth consciousness conditions the five aggregates of the past or future, this is a "solitary shadow-object" (*kevala-pratibimba-viṣaya*). On the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the perceiving consciousness, there is also a semblance-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), which is likewise called "carrying a substantial form.

When these three [conditions] combine within a single cause, the eighth consciousness conditions the "matter produced by meditative concentration" (*samādhi-nirmāṇa-rūpa*), which is the sphere of the noble ones (*ārya-gocara*). The mind-king (*citta-rāja*) conditions nature-objects and minds.

The objective referent (*ālambana*) is a solitary image (*pratibimba*). When it relies upon another's noble object as its substance, it is also "with-substance" (*sadravya*). Alternatively, there may be a difference in the nature of the seeds or their realm of attachment (*bandhana*):

for example, when a mind of a lower realm acts as the perceiver (*ālambaka*), taking the divine eye or ear of a higher realm as its object. Or, there may be identity in realm of attachment but difference in the nature of the seeds:

for example, when taking the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) of one's own realm as objects, whether belonging to oneself or others. Or, there may be identity in the nature of the seeds but difference in realm of attachment: for example, when the eighth consciousness perceives an object of a higher realm.

The divine eye, divine ear, and mind directly take their respective characteristics as objects, giving rise to "solitary-shadow" (duoying) objects; the mind-king (citta-rāja) takes these as its objects.
Although the "object-with-substance" (daizhi) [objects] differ in their inherent natures, the mind-king and the mental factors (caitta) are both of the same mental seed.
Regarding the meaning of the provisional self and dharmas: if there are only consciousnesses, how is it that worldly convention and the sacred teachings speak of a self and dharmas? Answer:

Because of the provisional designation of "self" and "dharmas," various appearances manifest. There are two kinds of worldly designations: first, those that lack intrinsic substance and follow [worldly] sentiment, which are provisionally established based on words.

This is the cause for arising the discourse on "self" (ātman) and "dharmas. Regarding that which is grasped as being entirely non-existent, it is designated as "self" and "dharmas. One interpretation states: based on the non-existent, there is a provisional designation of existence;

regarding the falsely imagined self and dharmas, the habitual tendencies (vāsanā) are treated as real, and thus they are designated as "sentient beings," "living beings," "realities," "qualities," and so forth—the five constant virtues and the two types of conventional existence in the holy teachings.
Another interpretation states: although they have no substantial essence, they are forcefully spoken of; this is a provisional designation based on words.
Although they exist, they are not real as previously described. True Suchness (tathatā) accords with conditions and establishes verbal teachings. One explanation states:

based on the meaning [of the principle] upon its substance, one provisionally relies on the transformed aspects and the seeing-nature to give rise to discourse; thereby, defilement is severed and purity is grasped, leading to the arising of true vision.

The twenty-seven noble beings (ārya) know suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, and cultivate the path. Regarding the cultivation of the path, there are those with sharp faculties and those with dull faculties. First, those resolved through faith (śraddhādhimukta); second, those attained through vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta).

In comparison to the path of vision of their own vehicle, those with sharp faculties enter the path of vision after three births, while those with dull faculties do so after sixty kalpas. Third, the stream-enterer (srotāpanna).

**Fruit:** The severance of the conceptualizations of the three realms; abandoning the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and entering the state of a noble one (*ārya*). This is called "stream-entry" (*srotāpanna*). 1. **Stream-enterer** (*srotāpanna*):

The stage prior to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), consisting of the first fifteen moments of mind. 2. **One who attains the first fruit after seven returns**: By the power of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), which are capable of sustaining seven births, one dies and is reborn seven times at most. 3. **Once-returner** (*sakṛdāgāmin*):

Having abandoned the first six categories of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation, or having arisen [in the higher realms] and severed [the remaining] without transcending the fruit. 4. **Candidate for once-returner** (*sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka*): Utilizing the sixth [category of abandonment].

The six paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the eleven moments of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) preceding them; the eight [stages of] *kulaṃkula* (family-to-family), who have abandoned the innate afflictions of the desire realm up to the first three categories and are called "three-birth" practitioners;

those who have abandoned up to the fourth category and are called "two-birth" *kulaṃkula*; the nine [stages of] the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*), who have abandoned the nine categories of innate afflictions of the desire realm and will no longer be reborn in the desire realm;
the ten [stages of] the candidate for non-returner (*anāgāmi-pratipannaka*); and the nine paths of uninterrupted transition and nine moments of liberation.
1. One who has transcended the previous seventeen mental states; 2. one who has attained bodily realization (*kāyasākṣin*) by abandoning the nine grades of innate afflictions of the desire realm;

3. one who has personally attained the four dhyānas and the eight stages of concentration; 4. one who is "with one interval" (*ekavicika*), having abandoned the lower and upper grades of innate afflictions and possessing only half a further birth after death;

5. one who is "not reborn in the realms" (*anāgāmin*), having abandoned seventy-two grades of afflictions of the two realms and transcending the cycle of birth and death through the stage of "transcendence."

14. Non-arising (*anutpāda*): This refers to the seventy-one moments of mind mentioned previously. 15. Parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*): One attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate existence;

this is not due to desire, nor is it the arising of the body of the prior existence (*pūrvakālabhava*). Because the fetters (*saṃyojana*) have already been exhausted, one is not born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); though the body arises, the fetters have already perished. 16. Single-type parinirvāṇa (*ekajātiparinirvāyin*):

Upon obtaining a body in the form realm, one immediately attains parinirvāṇa. 17. Parinirvāṇa through wisdom (*prajñāparinirvāyin*): One does not sever the hindrances to meditative concentration (*samādhyāvaraṇa*). Ten.
18. Parinirvāṇa with wisdom (saprājña-parinirvāyin): one who abandons the hindrance of concentration. 19. Parinirvāṇa without exertion (anabhisamskāra-parinirvāyin):

one who does not initiate effort, but by the power of past habituation, reaches the body of the form realm and realizes the fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa-phala). 20. Parinirvāṇa with exertion (sābhisamskāra-parinirvāyin): one who, relying on the body of the form realm, initiates effort and enters nirvana.

21. Upstream parinirvāṇa (ūrdhvasrotas-parinirvāyin): one who delights in wisdom and is born in the five Pure Abodes; delighting in meditative concentration, they are born in the formless realm. Second.
21. The one who falls away from the dharma (parihāna-dharman): they fall away from the bliss of the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukha*). 22. The one who contemplates the dharma (*cetana-dharman*):
by means of contemplation, they do not fall away from the bliss of the present life. 23. The one who guards the dharma (*anurakṣaṇā-dharman*): if they do not guard it, they immediately lose it. 24.

The one who abides in the dharma (*sthitākampya-dharman*): they are unable to transform dullness into sharpness. 25. The one who is capable of penetration (*prativedhanā-dharman*): their concentration and wisdom are balanced and equal; they sever... [the fetters].
The inferior attainment. Twenty-seven types of those who dwell in the immovable parinirvāṇa, who are not moved by afflictions or habitual tendencies. The verse says:
